title: A Fun Way To Assess Your Class, Have A Good Laugh, And Build Everlasting Rapport d-laugh-and-build-everlasting-rapport/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a playful strategy for assessing how well students understand classroom routines: showing up disguised as a substitute character (in his case, a surfer-dude alter ego named 'Mr. Kahuna'). By pretending to be new and asking students to explain everything—from morning routines to the classroom management plan—the teacher can see, through their explanations, how thoroughly expectations have been internalized. He notes the dual purpose is genuine fun and memory-building alongside an authentic assessment disguised as play. He cautions the strategy isn't for every teacher or grade level, but the underlying principle—injecting more fun to widen the gap between the appeal of the classroom and the unattractiveness of consequences—applies broadly.
points: Wider contrast between how much students enjoy the classroom and how much they dislike time-out is described as 'the holy grail of classroom management.'
Adopting a temporary substitute-teacher persona lets students 'teach back' routines and expectations, revealing how well they actually understand them.
The strategy should only be used once a class has proven ready for it—not early in the year before trust and consistency are established.
The exercise doubles as assessment and memory-making, deepening rapport through shared fun rather than didactic instruction.
More fun in the classroom is framed as a direct lever for reducing misbehavior, not a distraction from managing it.
quotes: The secret to exceptional classroom management is a learning experience your students love and want to be part of combined with a consistently followed classroom management plan.

The widening contrast between these two core principles—that is, how much your students enjoy being a member of your classroom and how averse they are toward time-out—is the holy grail of classroom management.
I’d put on a blond wig and board shorts and show up to meet my students at their line first thing in the morning.
In a strange and wonderful way, it’s like being a fly on the wall of your own classroom. It’s a remarkably satisfying experience
The power to curb misbehavior comes not from harsher consequences or humiliating scoldings and talking-tos, but from the simple joy of being a valued member of your classroom.
